Horror has always been a stress test for masculinity. The genre sets up men as protectors, rational problem solvers, and keepers of control, then spends ninety minutes dismantling each of those roles. The macho hero who splits off from the group to prove he doesnât need anyone is usually the first to die, which makes the genre quietly skeptical of the whole performance. Monsters often work as mirrors here too. Think of the slasher, a figure of unchecked male rage and entitlement, or the werewolf, where aggression literally takes over the body. Meanwhile the âfinal girlâ tradition tends to flip the script by rewarding vigilance, empathy, and adaptability over brute force, which are traits the genre treats as strengths rather than weaknesses.

More recent horror has gotten more honest about what men fear when the rules stop working. Films about fatherhood, grief, and emotional isolation show male characters undone not by a creature but by their inability to talk about what scares them. The monster becomes a stand-in for everything unspoken, and survival depends on vulnerability rather than dominance. Folklore does this too. Many cryptid and campfire legends center on men who wander into the woods alone, ignore warnings, and meet something that doesnât care how tough they think they are. At its best, horror gives men a safe place to be afraid, and the stories that stick are the ones where fear gets confronted instead of performed.

I personally own the roadmap for reducing false negatives in the âPre-Hostile Civilianâ category. I know what this sounds like. I know what Palantir does. I know what ICE does. I know what the United States military does. My claim is that, once you stop doing ethics on a five-year time horizon, this is probably the most left-wing job I could have.

The mistake people make is evaluating HAYFORK according to who controls it in 2026 rather than its expected utility across the full future light cone. Assume there is even a 0.3 percent chance that some descendant of the administrative infrastructure we are building survives the transition out of capitalism. Now multiply a small improvement in state capacity by ten billion people, hundreds or thousands of years, and eventual extraterrestrial settlement. A system that currently helps an imperial state decide which households to target could someday help a planetary peopleâs republic identify famine three weeks earlier, route medicine to every diabetic in Chengdu, relocate coastal populations before a typhoon, or allocate protein during a nuclear winter. At that scale, refusing to improve the ontology because you dislike its present deployment means sacrificing trillions of unborn people to preserve your personal moral cleanliness during one extremely short historical interval.

A common objection to taking my grandmotherâs pain pills is that they are prescribed to her, stored in her home, and intended for her pain. All three observations are true but decision-theoretically incomplete. Property rights are a useful heuristic; they are not a substitute for comparing marginal utility across agents.

My grandmother uses the pills only when her pain exceeds some internal threshold. I, by contrast, experience a reliable and immediate improvement in mood whenever I know there are controlled substances available to me. Her benefit is therefore intermittent and state-dependent, while mine includes a persistent option value. Any serious analysis should count both.

Let the expected utility of reallocating one pill be:

EU = M + O + Q â G â L

M = immediate marginal utility to me
O = option value of possession
Q = household efficiency gained by reducing idle pharmaceutical inventory
G = expected increase in my grandmotherâs future pain
L = legal, medical, familial, and reputational loss
The neglected term is O. Critics treat a pill sitting in a bathroom cabinet as if it were already producing welfare. It is not. It is inventory. My grandmother may need it later; I can value having it now. The mere fact that her potential claim is medically legitimate does not make its probability one.

There is also a timing asymmetry. Her pain is stochastic and future. My desire is certain and present. Standard discounting therefore favors me unless one quietly inserts a large grandmother-specific moral coefficient. That coefficient may be defensible, but it should be stated rather than smuggled into the analysis under emotionally loaded words like âstealing.â
